 The 2027 Social Security COLA Is Official - Here’s Exactly How Much More You’ll Get
 Find out what the 3.6% COLA means for your monthly check.
 By
 David Maina, CPA 
 ,
 Edited by
 Laura Hohenstein 
 Updated
 Oct. 20, 2026
 Fact checked 
 This article was subjected to a comprehensive fact-checking process. Our professional fact-checkers verify article information against primary sources, reputable publishers, and experts in the field.
 Add Us On Google
 Google Preferred Sources lets you customize your search results. By choosing to follow FinanceBuzz, you’re telling Google to prioritize content from a source you trust.
The numbers are finally in, and Social Security recipients have a slightly bigger raise to look forward to next year. The Social Security Administration has announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for 2027, up from the 2.8% increase in 2026. 
If you're living on just Social Security , even an extra $50 or $70 a month could help make your check go a little further. And if you have other retirement income, the raise could help you cover rising expenses without dipping as much into your savings. 
Here's how much more Social Security will pay in 2027 and when you can expect to receive your raise.

 Who can expect a bigger Social Security check in 2027
Around 72 million Social Security recipients will get a 3.6% increase in 2027, according to the Social Security Administration. The raise applies to retirement, survivor, and disability benefits, and when you include people receiving Supplemental Security Income (SSI), roughly 76 million Americans will benefit. 
How much extra you'll receive depends on your current benefit, with the average monthly increases expected to look like this: 
 Retired workers: $2,095 to $2,170, up $75 a month.
 Disabled workers: $1,642 to $1,701, up $59 a month.
 Widows and widowers living alone: $1,936 to $2,005, up $69 a month.
Your own raise could be higher or lower depending on what you currently receive, but the 3.6% adjustment applies to everyone eligible for the increase.

 Here's how much a $2,000 Social Security check will grow
To estimate your new monthly amount, simply multiply your current benefit by 1.036. Here's what the raise could look like depending on how much you receive now:

If you receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI), the maximum federal payment will also increase in 2027, rising from $994 to $1,029 a month for an individual and from $1,491 to $1,544 for an eligible couple. Your actual SSI payment may be lower depending on your income and living arrangements. 
 When you'll receive your bigger Social Security check
Your 3.6% raise will start with your December 2026 benefits, which Social Security pays in January 2027. So if you're receiving retirement benefits, you can expect the extra money to arrive on your usual payment date in January. 
For most retirees, that date depends on when you were born: 
 Born on the 1st through the 10th: January 13, 2027.
 Born on the 11th through the 20th: January 20, 2027.
 Born on the 21st through the 31st: January 27, 2027.
If you receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI), you'll get your increase a little earlier. Since January 1 is a federal holiday, your first higher payment will arrive on December 31, 2026, just in time for the new year.

 Why your Social Security deposit could be smaller than expected
Your Social Security benefit may be getting a 3.6% raise, but the amount that actually reaches your bank account could increase by a little less. Social Security uses its own rounding rules when calculating your new benefit, so the final figure may differ slightly from a simple percentage calculation. 
And if your Medicare Part B premium is deducted from your Social Security check, any increase in that premium could eat into your raise before you receive it. You'll still get the 3.6% adjustment to your benefits, but you may have less of that extra money left to spend than you expected. 
 How to find out exactly how much you'll get in 2027
You should be able to find out exactly how much your Social Security check will increase by late November, when the SSA starts posting personalized COLA notices in the Message Center of your my Social Security account. 
Your notice will show your new benefit amount, along with any deductions, so you'll have a better idea of how much money will actually reach your bank account. 
If you'd prefer to get your notice online, you'll generally need to have an account set up and choose paperless notifications by November 18. Otherwise, you can expect a letter in the mail in December. 
In the meantime, multiplying your current benefit by 1.036 can give you a good estimate of what to expect, so you can start planning your budget for next year. 
 Bottom line
A 3.6% raise won't make rising prices disappear, but it's still a little more money to work with each month. Whether it helps with your grocery bill or an expense you've been putting off, those extra dollars could take some of the strain off your budget. 
Once your personalized COLA notice arrives, you'll know how much of the raise you'll actually receive after deductions. From there, you can work the amount into your retirement plan and decide where it'll do the most good. Even a small increase can make life a little easier when you know exactly what you have to spend.
